scenes.text: So, how do you check what the evidence says? Here are four statements about how skills improve. All four get repeated everywhere. A: it takes ten thousand hours of practice to become an expert. B: practising skills in a shuffled order makes practice look worse, and retention better. C: kids who want to reach the top should specialise in one sport early. D: visualising a skill works as well as practising it. Only one of these is a research finding as stated. Which one? And what's wrong with the other three?

Researching a skill starts with the question, and earlier you saw that the question decides everything after it. How do you get better at netball? That returns everything ever written, and answers nothing. How is shooting developed in netball? Better, but findings will clash, because they're about different learners. Here's a question you can research: how should practice be arranged to improve shooting under pressure, for teenage club netballers? It names the sport, the skill, the part of the skill, and who it's for. Pick a skill you can actually go and watch this week.

Sources don't deserve equal weight, so rank them. At the top is a systematic review, which gathers every study on a question by a stated method. Next, a peer-reviewed study, checked by other researchers before it's published. Then textbooks and sporting bodies, accurate but often a few years behind. Then coaching magazines and journalism, written to be interesting, so the finding often sounds stronger than the study. And at the bottom, social media and coach opinion. Low doesn't mean worthless. A coach's opinion is weak evidence about what works, but strong evidence about what coaches do. Then ask four questions of any source. Who was studied? How many? Who paid for it? And is this the study, or someone's account of it?

Now the four statements. Each one sits on real research, and three have been stretched. A: the real study found the best violinists had averaged about ten thousand hours of deliberate practice, effortful work on weaknesses with feedback, by about age twenty. An average became a requirement, and deliberate practice became just hours. C: elite athletes often did specialise early. But the ones who specialised and quit were never counted. That's a correlation, two things going together, read as a cause. Studies that follow everyone tend to favour trying several sports. D: visualising does help, alongside real practice, once you have a movement to rehearse. The qualifier got dropped. And the fourth stretch is a result from a narrow sample, say twelve elite adults, sold as true for everyone. B is the real finding. It's specific, it admits its own cost, and it's inconvenient: it tells coaches the better session looks worse. Convenient, round-numbered claims deserve the most suspicion. Even so, in real sport settings the effect is smaller than in the lab.

The syllabus asks how research is applied in practice. "Coaches should vary their practice" isn't an application. It's the finding with should added. An application is something you could photograph. Take the netball question. To acquire the shot, blocked practice while the pattern forms. To develop it, shuffle the three shooting drills by a called number instead of blocks of ten. To improve it, swap the cone for a live defender, so she has to choose between shooting and passing. Then add a limit. A session that looks worse can get dropped in a fortnight, and a finding from adult students might not hold for teenagers.

Then propose further research questions, which shows you actually read. Good questions come from four places. The sample: does this hold for fourteen-year-old beginners, not adults? A disagreement: why does mixed practice help in one study and not another? The measure: retention was tested after a day, so does it last a season? And the practice gap: if the evidence is clear, why don't coaches use it? Often it's because it looks worse and is harder to run. And report gaps honestly. If you found little on your skill, or a claim you couldn't trace to any study, say so. That's a finding too.
Two things to remember. Rank by evidence, not by confidence. And an application is something you could photograph.

Two exam questions. First. A social media post says research shows ten minutes of juggling a day doubles junior footballers' passing accuracy. The study it links to tested fourteen adult university students for two weeks. Identify two weaknesses in using this post as evidence for a junior team. Pause here to answer.

First, the sample. Fourteen adult students aren't junior footballers, so it may not generalise. Second, the source. A post is someone's account, at the bottom of the ladder, and "doubles" may be stronger than the study found. Also, two weeks shows performance, not lasting learning. The classic mistake is saying "it's not peer-reviewed" without saying why it matters.

Second. A study of adult beginners suggests they learn a tiring skill better with distributed practice. A swimming club teaches beginners butterfly in one ninety-minute session each Saturday. Apply this finding to the club's sessions, name one constraint, and propose one further research question. Pause here to answer.

Apply it as something you could photograph: short butterfly sets of two lengths, with real rest, spread through the session, or split across two shorter sessions a week. Constraint: pool time and coaches may only be available on Saturday. Further question, from the sample: does this hold for children, not the adults studied? The classic mistake is writing "use distributed practice" and stopping.

So, for any skill, narrow the question, rank the sources, check for the four stretches, apply it to a real session, and ask what's still unknown. That's how skills are learnt and checked. But a skill only grows if someone keeps turning up to practise it. And no ladder answers that one. Why is staying in sport harder than starting?
